Abu Amir has an arrow drawn from his knee and the Prophet asks forgiveness for him; Sa'd comes armed at night to guard the Prophet, who then sleeps.
May the slave of dinar, dirham and fine clothes, pleased only when given, perish, while Paradise is for the dusty fighter holding his horse's reins, content at front or rear.
An older companion serves Anas, having vowed to serve any Ansari; Anas serves the Prophet; those not fasting serve and take the reward; helping a rider is charity.
Guarding Muslims from unbelievers for one day in Allah's cause, a whip's space in Paradise, and a morning or evening journey in His cause are each better than the world.
Serving the Prophet on the Khaibar expedition, Anas hears his prayers for refuge, sees him marry Safiya with a feast of hais, and hears him make Medina a sanctuary.
Waking from a nap, the Prophet tells Umm Haram of followers voyaging like kings on thrones, she among the first; returning from jihad, she falls and breaks her neck.
Sa'd is told victory and provision come only through the poor among them; armies are given victory while one among them has accompanied the Prophet, then his companions, then theirs.
A fierce fighter the Prophet places among the people of the Fire kills himself when wounded; one may seem to do Paradise's deeds yet belong to the Fire.
The Prophet urges Bani Aslam to practise archery, as their father Ishmael was an archer, and at Badr orders arrows shot when the enemy comes near.
When Umar hits Ethiopians playing before the Prophet with a stone, the Prophet tells him to let them play; a sub-narrator adds that this was in the mosque.
The Prophet shares Abu Talha's shield, and Fatima stops his bleeding when his helmet is smashed; Bani an-Nadir's fai buys arms and horses; Sa'd is urged to shoot.
On Eid the Prophet tells Abu Bakr to leave two girls singing songs of Bu'ath, and lets Aisha watch from behind him as Bani Arfida play with shields and spears.
The Prophet rides with a sword at his neck; conquerors' swords bore no gold or silver; a bedouin who seized his sword is spared; Abu Qatada spears an onager.
In his tent at Badr, in armour, the Prophet pleads for Allah's promise until Abu Bakr says it is enough, then goes out reciting that the multitude will be routed.
The Prophet died while his iron armour was mortgaged to a Jew for thirty sa' of barley.
The miser and the charitable are like two men in tight iron cloaks: giving spreads the giver's cloak over him, while the miser's rings tighten and will not widen.
After relieving himself, the Prophet made ablution in a tight-sleeved Sha'mi cloak, drawing his arms out from beneath it, and wiped over his head and leather socks.
The Prophet allowed Abdur-Rahman bin Auf and az-Zubair to wear silk because of itching from a skin disease or lice, and they wore it in battle.
The Prophet ate from a sheep's shoulder, cutting it with a knife, then put the knife down when called and prayed without repeating his ablution.
Paradise awaits the Prophet's first followers to sail on expedition, Umm Haram among them; the first army to invade Caesar's City is forgiven, but she is not in it.
Before the Hour Muslims will fight the Jews until a stone tells of a Jew hiding behind it, and fight the Turks, small-eyed and flat-nosed, and people in hair shoes.
The Prophet seeks victory at Hunain, invokes fire and defeat on the Clans, prays for weak Muslims, against Mudar and named men of Quraish, and answers Jews' death-wish in kind.
The Prophet writes to Caesar that rejecting Islam brings his people's sins on him, prays for Daus's guidance, seals letters with a silver ring, and Khusrau tears up his letter.
The Prophet's letter invites Caesar to Islam; Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan, finds in his answers the qualities of a prophet, and his court breaks into uproar.
At Khaibar the Prophet cures Ali's eyes, gives him the flag and tells him to invite them to Islam first, one convert through him being better than red camels.
The Prophet attacked only after dawn, holding back if he heard the adhan; reaching Khaibar by night, he attacked at daybreak, saying Khaibar is ruined.
The Prophet was ordered to fight people until they say none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, which saves their life and property, their account resting with Allah.
Before campaigns the Prophet hid his real destination, except for Tabuk, a long march in great heat against a large enemy, when he told the Muslims so they could prepare.
The Prophet usually set out on Thursdays, Tabuk included; he set out after Zuhr at Medina, five days before Dhul Qa'da ended for Hajj, and in Ramadan, fasting until Kadid.
Sending an expedition, the Prophet first orders two named men of Quraish burnt, then withdraws it at the farewell: only Allah punishes with fire, so kill them if captured.
Obey the ruler except in disobedience to Allah; obeying the Prophet is obeying Allah, obeying the chief is obeying him, and the Imam is a shield to fight behind.
Companions recall pledging allegiance to the Prophet under the tree, for patience or death, the Ansar for jihad at the Trench, and, migration being over, for Islam and jihad.
Asked whether to obey a commander ordering what they cannot do, Abdullah says he does not know, but one stays well while obeying Allah and should ask about doubtful things.
The Prophet told the people not to wish to meet the enemy but be patient when they do, for Paradise is under swords' shade, and asked Allah to defeat them.
On a campaign the Prophet's prayer speeds Jabir's tired camel; he buys it, letting Jabir ride it home, hears why he wed a matron, then pays and returns it.
When Medina was alarmed the Prophet rode Abu Talha's horse out alone, found nothing to fear, and said the horse, once slow, was very fast.
Umar gave a horse for Allah's Cause and later saw it being sold; the Prophet told him not to buy it, as that would take back his charity.
The Prophet would join every army unit but lacks mounts for his followers and dislikes them staying behind; he wishes to be martyred in Allah's Cause, revived and martyred again.
At Tabuk, Yali gives a camel for jihad; his hired worker's quarrel ends with a bitten hand pulled free and a tooth lost, and the Prophet rejects the biter's claim.
Flag-bearer Qais bin Sa'd combs his hair for Hajj; at Khaibar the flag goes to Ali, who came despite eye trouble; Az-Zubair is told where to fix the flag.
